Before we move ahead with today's agenda, I wish to communicate my ruling in response to the point of order raised by Heledd Fychan MS at the end of the meeting on 23 September 2026. I have had an opportunity to review the Record of Proceedings. My ruling is that the contribution made by Joe Martin MS to the short debate on 23 September breached Standing Order 13.9(v), as it constituted

'disorderly, discriminatory or offensive language or language which detracts from the dignity of the Senedd'.

I want to make it clear that Members of the Senedd are entitled to hold and express strong and differing views. I will defend the rights of all Members to express their perspectives and to challenge that of other Members. It is the nature of parliamentary debate that Members will frequently disagree, and often in a robust manner. However, contributions must comply with the Standing Orders and the required standards of conduct in a parliamentary setting. And they must be grounded in respect for others at all times. This ruling concerns the language used and the manner in which the contribution was expressed, rather than the right to debate the subject matter.

I have written to Joe Martin concerning my ruling, and to require that he ensures that the language used meets the requirements of order and respect in future. That is my ruling.

Diolch, Brif Weinidog. The right to information is meaningless if citizens have to fight public bodies to simply obtain information that they're legally entitled to. Your own Government recognises the statutory deadlines for freedom of information and subject access requests. 

So, I have a very simple question: does the Welsh Government actually monitor whether devolved public bodies in Wales are complying with those legal obligations, and, if so, will you publish that information? Because, if your Government doesn't even know which public bodies are repeatedly failing to comply with the public's right to information, how can you credibly claim that transparency in Wales is being reinforced, rather than merely advertised?

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Brif Weinidog. The local government settlement for the current financial year was finalised under the previous Welsh Labour Government, following extensive engagement with local authorities. This used an established formula of complex indicators, including population density, service demand and levels of poverty and deprivation, and work was going on to ensure that that was all updated. The local authorities who received the largest annual increase in funding based on that set formula were Newport, Swansea, Blaenau Gwent, Wrexham and Merthyr Tydfil. First Minister, can you confirm which local authorities will not receive extra funding to tackle poverty?

There are issues of deprivation that are predominantly urban in nature, there are issues of deprivation that are predominantly rural in nature, and there are issues of deprivation that are equally relevant to both. contributions.text_english: First Minister, councils are being asked to do more every year, but with less. Westminster made them responsible for social care. In Cardiff Bay, new statutory duties keep on coming, and other costs are building up. Swansea Council has already set aside £28 million for equal pay claims. That's £28 million not being spent on schools, not being spent on our roads, and not being spent on social care. Similar claims have already bankrupted Birmingham City Council. These are legally binding costs, yet the formula that shares out local government funding was never designed to account for them. So, First Minister, what consideration is being given to these huge costs in the funding formula, and will you commit that no new duties will be placed on councils without the money to deliver them? Otherwise, it is local services that will be cut.

What's important to me is that we as a Government work very, very closely with local government, which my Cabinet Minister for local government does day in, day out, recognising the pressures that do exist, taking into consideration always how the decisions and actions and ambitions of this Government do place responsibilities not just on the Welsh Government itself, but on our partners throughout Wales. It is by working together cleverly that we can try to work through that on behalf of the people that we represent.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, I certainly agree with the comments made by colleagues across the Chamber here so far, because local authorities, councils, and the work they do is the lifeblood of our communities, from the roads that we drive on to the schools that we send our children to. contributions.text_english: It's very important that local authorities are able to make their own decisions on local taxation. It's a great start, but there are more steps that can be taken, I believe, by the UK Government. Last week, I attended an event with Music Venue Trust, which highlighted the issue of value added tax. Thank you, First Minister. Wales does need a secure long-term supply of aggregates if we are to deliver the homes, schools, and transport infrastructure our communities need. The Welsh Government has long said that the use of secondary and recycled materials should be maximised where practical, and high-quality washed recycled aggregates allow us to do exactly that, turning construction and demolition waste into material that meets the same standards as quarried stone and sand, reducing pressure on primary extraction and on marine dredge sand, and cutting carbon all along the way, which is good.

There appears, however, to be a disconnect between Wales's circular economy ambitions and public sector procurement in practice at the moment. We have seen local authority works taking place directly outside a recycling plant in Cwmgwili, where virgin aggregate was sourced from a quarry 20 miles away rather than the actual aggregate that was at that plant, which seems ridiculous. We now need action, not words. So, First Minister, what further steps will Welsh Government take through procurement, planning and its own capital programmes to increase the use of washed recycled aggregates in construction projects in Wales?

I'd like to request a statement on the well-being outcomes for care leavers in Wales. Last month, the UK Department of Education published 'You really are on your own', a study of the early deaths of young people who were in care, and its findings are deeply concerning. In 2025 alone, 112 care leavers aged 18 to 24 died in England, an estimated death rate around three to four times that of their peers in the general population. One in five of those deaths occurred at age 18, right when support so often fails and falls away. The report must serve as a warning for us here in Wales.

Care-experienced young people have consistently raised here many of the issues around isolation, cliff edges in support, and independence being treated as more important than well-being. So, may I ask, please, Trefnydd, what can we do here in Wales to make sure we've got the data on young people and make sure we've got the services in place to support them? Diolch yn fawr iawn.

Thank you very much, Llywydd. I'm pleased to provide an update on the commitment in our first 100-day plan to commission a review of the effectiveness of the NHS Wales escalation and intervention framework.

The review was commissioned to ensure that our arrangements for accountability, oversight, support and intervention remain fit for purpose in a healthcare environment that is increasingly complex. Discussions with NHS organisations in recent months have reinforced the need for a framework that is clearer, more consistent, and more focused on securing sustainable improvement.

The review found that escalation and intervention arrangements provided an important mechanism for identifying concerns, strengthening oversight, and deploying targeted support where necessary. However, the review also found opportunities to strengthen the connection between routine accountability processes and formal intervention arrangements.

In particular, there was a desire to move away from a system that is perceived primarily through the lens of escalation levels to a new system, a system that places greater emphasis on continuous assessment and early intervention, helping organisations to improve and ultimately ensure better outcomes for patients.

Today, we publish a new accountability and support framework, which provides a single, coherent approach to deal with accountability, assurance, support and intervention across NHS Wales. It establishes a more transparent and structured framework that will help the Welsh Government and NHS organisations to assess how they are performing, identify emerging risks, and agree the responses required to support improvement. It also clarifies better the relationship between accountability meetings, routine performance oversight, improvement support and intervention activity.

Can I welcome to your post and congratulate you on your appointment as shadow spokesperson for health and care, and good luck with it, and thank your predecessor as well for his contributions? 

I welcome the fact that you see the value of what we've put forward here, and that you welcome much of what we've put forward. And I would hope that we would have cross-party support for what we are hoping to achieve here. You mentioned putting outcomes at the centre of what we want to achieve, that workforce is important and that we take proactive action, which is all about making sure that we deal with issues before they become major problems that impact on the health outcomes of our people. But you did raise some questions and I'll try my best to respond to as many of them as I can in the few minutes I have.

The blurred lines you mentioned between civil servants and the Minister; ultimately, my civil servants and officials have meetings regularly with health boards on a weekly basis, and the director general of the NHS will have regular meetings with the chief executive of health boards.

When it comes to an escalated level and when we need to look at specific issues within health boards, then the agreement on how we escalate them and which matters need to be looked at will be come to between Audit Wales, Healthcare Inspectorate Wales, Welsh Government and the health boards themselves, so that they are an equal partner in this, that they realise what the issues are, and that they come up with solutions with other partners and stakeholders. Then, the work will be led by NHS Wales Performance and Improvement.

Now, NHS performance and improvement will lead that work, but going on to another question you asked about ensuring that lessons are learnt, they will then take those lessons and in another health board—or a trust if an issue arises—they will take those lessons and use them in the learnings for the problems that might arise in other health boards.

The assessments that you mentioned and what criteria will be set will be judged by those stakeholders, including the health boards, but they will be transparent so that people can have confidence in the process. We know in the previous process, it was accused of being used as a political weapon more often than not. This shouldn't be about politics—this should be about making sure that health boards improve if they have problems and de-escalate when they can, so that people can have confidence in the health care that they receive.

So, the process will be transparent, assessments will be made by the stakeholders transparently, collectively, and then the de-escalation process will also be transparent and show accountability for the process, and how they have come to the judgements they've got for de-escalation purposes.

I think that responds—the final criteria lines—yes, I think that's responded to most of the questions you asked, at least.
